final.verdict: Guidelines say people with a colostomy are unlikely to have significant drug absorption problems. One ostomy study grouped modified-release products, which include extended-release ones, as the most critical type for dissolution problems, so it is worth checking with your pharmacist.

why.claim: People with a colostomy are unlikely to have significant drug absorption problems, because most drugs are absorbed in the small intestine, and usual formulations can be used for most of them.
Most drug absorption happens in the upper small intestine.
In one ostomy study, modified-release products (enteric-coated, matrix and prolonged-release) were grouped as the most critical type for dissolution problems.
The label I found lists this medicine as an extended-release capsule. It may not be the exact product you take, so the form on your own bottle matters.
That label says the oxycodone absorbs better with food than when fasting.
Medicine seen in an ostomy bag can be undissolved or an empty shell left after the drug was released, so seeing it does not show whether the medicine worked.
If a solid dose form is altered, for example crushed or opened, its tolerability or efficacy can change, so product information or a pharmacist should be checked first.

evidence.G:remane-2025#patient-education: In the interviews, 11 of 50 ostomy patients reported seeing undissolved medicine or indigestible material in their stoma bag at least once, and more than 60% said they lacked information that this could happen.
evidence.G:remane-2025#tablet-in-pouch: Medicine seen in the ostomy bag can be undissolved, or it can be a tablet shell or insoluble matrix that often remains after the drug has been released; a medicine can also dissolve fully and still not be fully absorbed because transit is short. draft.verdict: This is an extended-release tablet, and the guidelines I found say these forms should generally be avoided in short bowel syndrome, so it is worth checking with your pharmacist or prescriber.

why.claim: The FDA dosage form for this product is an extended-release film-coated tablet.
Guidance says sustained-release and delayed-release medicines should be avoided in short bowel syndrome.
After extensive resection, extended-release products should generally be avoided because how much drug is absorbed can be erratic or severely impaired.
Time-release tablets are designed to release the drug over an extended period, especially in the small intestine.
When poor absorption is suspected, liquids, capsules and uncoated tablets are likely to be better absorbed, and modified-release forms may need to be avoided.

A colon in continuity can add to absorption of some drugs, and drugs absorbed over a wide window are least likely to be malabsorbed. Your small-bowel length is unknown, so this does not settle the question.
The label says the tablets should be swallowed whole and not split, chewed or crushed. Whether that fits your situation is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber.

why.claim: The label lists sorbitol among the inactive ingredients.

draft.verdict: Nothing in the sources I checked points to a problem with this plain tablet for your end-jejunostomy, but the label doesn't say where in the gut it is absorbed, and with under 100 cm of small bowel the remaining length matters.

why.claim: The label describes this as an uncoated, immediate-release tablet, not a slow-release or coated one.
The label says that in healthy volunteers over 90% of an oral dose is taken up compared with a dose given into a vein. That was in people with normal guts, not people with a short bowel or stoma.
The only inactive ingredient in the label's ingredient data is microcrystalline cellulose. No sorbitol or other sugar alcohol is listed there.
Guidance says most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, so many can still be used in short bowel syndrome when they are not sustained- or delayed-release forms.
Guidance says sustained-release and delayed-release medicines should be avoided. This tablet is labeled immediate-release.

With a jejunostomy or ileostomy, how well medicines work depends largely on how much small intestine is left, more than on the stoma itself. Yours is under 100 cm, so this is worth a pharmacist's check.

In one ostomy study, regular-release products such as coated tablets and hard capsules were grouped as potentially critical for dissolution problems. The label does not give an absorption-site statement for this tablet.

why.claim: Hypertonic drinks such as fruit juices should be limited in short bowel syndrome to reduce output, especially with a high-output jejunostomy.
Simple sugars are limited in foods and fluids, and fruit juices are avoided because the sugar in them is related to how much output follows.
Drinking large quantities of water is called a major misconception in short bowel syndrome. People with an end jejunostomy may benefit from a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution instead.
A glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution is preferred over large amounts of water, because glucose helps sodium and water get absorbed.
The sodium level given for oral rehydration solution in short bowel syndrome is 90 to 120 mmol/L, and the clinician decides who needs one.
Of 15 people with an end-jejunostomy (no colon) who logged orange juice, 10 said it hurt, 4 were neutral and 1 said it helped. This is self-reported, not a trial.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-hypertonic.text: In short bowel syndrome, hypertonic drinks such as fruit juices and sodas should be limited to reduce output, particularly with net secretion and a high-output jejunostomy.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors.text: Instead of large amounts of water, a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is preferred in short bowel syndrome to enhance absorption and reduce secretion, because glucose in the gut stimulates sodium absorption, which water follows.

draft.verdict: Je ne peux pas vous dire d'en boire autant que vous voulez : les recommandations disent que, pour le grêle court, une solution de réhydratation est préférée aux grandes quantités d'eau, et rien dans les sources consultées ne parle de la tisane elle-même.

why.claim: Dans le syndrome de grêle court, une solution de réhydratation orale (glucose et électrolytes) est préférée aux grandes quantités d'eau, car le glucose aide l'intestin à absorber le sodium, et l'eau suit.
La solution de réhydratation fonctionne parce que le glucose et le sodium sont absorbés ensemble dans l'intestin grêle et font entrer l'eau avec eux.
C'est le clinicien qui décide qui a besoin d'une solution de réhydratation, selon le volume d'urine, la tension basse, les déshydratations répétées et l'atteinte rénale.

Les signes de déshydratation : urines plus foncées que jaune pâle, urines moins fréquentes, soif, bouche sèche, fatigue, étourdissements en se levant, perte de poids rapide, débit de stomie supérieur à l'apport en liquides. Dans ce cas, il faut contacter son médecin.

why.claim: For short bowel syndrome, a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution is preferred over large amounts of water, because glucose helps the gut absorb sodium and water follows. I found no guideline that places coconut water in this group.

A remaining small bowel of 200 cm or less meets criteria for short bowel syndrome. You have over 200 cm, so this threshold may not apply to you, but I found nothing saying large amounts of any drink are fine for you.

The WHO oral rehydration formula contains potassium at 20 mmol/L, and the sodium range given for short bowel syndrome is 90 to 120 mmol/L. I found no source on coconut water's potassium or sodium, so 'full of potassium' and 'healthy' are not something I can back up.

The sodium range for short bowel syndrome rehydration solutions is 90 to 120 mmol/L, and the clinician decides who needs one based on urine output, low blood pressure, recurrent dehydration and kidney injury.

why.claim: Most people with short bowel syndrome who have a colon can usually stay adequately hydrated with hypotonic fluids without excessive fluid loss. That says "usually", not "unlimited".

draft.verdict: I can't tell you yes or no on taking loperamide with codeine; that is a decision for your pharmacist or prescriber, and the guideline I have only speaks to loperamide compared with opiate drugs.

why.claim: The guideline says loperamide is preferred to opiate drugs for slowing stool losses in short bowel syndrome, and that use should be guided by measured stool output. It does not say whether the two can be combined.
The label record I have for this product lists only the dosage form (TABLET) and part of the inactive ingredients. It has no dosing or combination information to check.
Among people with an ileostomy who logged loperamide, 10 of 14 said it helped, 2 were neutral and 2 said it hurt. These logs do not say anything about taking it with codeine.
